title: Sorting Algorithms
learning_outcomes: Explain the main idea behind sorting algorithms in your own words.
Apply sorting algorithms to a minimal C example and predict the result.
Identify a relevant boundary, portability assumption, or failure mode.

content.intro: This lesson explores Sorting Algorithms through an original visual, a compact C example and a check you can perform locally.
content.why_it_matters: Understanding sorting algorithms helps you reason about C programs rather than relying on trial and error. It also helps you communicate assumptions, write safer code, and debug behavior across toolchains.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
Sorting Algorithms is studied as part of **Algorithms and Data Structures in C**. Start with the contract: identify the inputs or program state, the rule C applies, and the observable result. Then check the behavior in a small, repeatable example.

The source curriculum also lists: Bubble sort and insertion sort, Selection sort, Merge sort and quicksort. Keep these subtopics connected to the parent concept rather than treating them as unrelated trivia.

In C, details can depend on the selected language standard and implementation. Distinguish defined behavior from unspecified, implementation-defined, or undefined behavior, and consult the cited standard/compiler references when portability matters.

content_blocks.title: Practical reasoning
content_blocks.text: For “Sorting Algorithms”, write down the preconditions first. Identify valid inputs and boundaries, decide which C rule applies, then choose evidence that would falsify your assumption. Prefer a small test with a clear expected result and compile with diagnostics enabled.

content_blocks.title: Search and data structures
content_blocks.run_instructions: Specify edge cases (empty collection, duplicate values, not-found target) and choose an algorithm based on preconditions and complexity.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original example, rebuild with the same compiler flags, rerun the same inputs, and compare actual output with the stated result. For time-, platform-, or input-dependent examples, record the environment and do not expect identical values everywhere.
content_blocks.limitations: The CodeLeaf lesson page does not run C code. Compile locally or use a separately deployed, isolated C runner; do not execute arbitrary learner code inside FastAPI.

content_blocks.title: Portability and safety check
content_blocks.text: Use a documented standard mode; treat compiler extensions as extensions, not ISO C guarantees. Check return values, buffer bounds, and object lifetime. This course example is draft material and needs code review on the target toolchain before publication.

task: In a scratch file, create one small example that demonstrates sorting algorithms. Explain the expected result before running it, compile with warnings enabled, and record one boundary case or portability question.
hints: Reduce the program to the smallest example that still shows the concept.
Write down the input, expected result, and assumptions before running it.
Check the official language/compiler reference and test a boundary case.
expected_output: A short, reproducible C example and explanation showing sorting algorithms, plus a note about one boundary or portability consideration.
common_mistakes: Treating sorting algorithms as a rule to memorize rather than a behavior to test.
Ignoring compiler warnings, input validity, or object lifetime.
Assuming behavior observed on one compiler is guaranteed by every C implementation.
